part.reserve.title: Spare tempo
part.reserve.summary: A pawn advance that does not harm the position passes the turn without moving the kings: with it, the opposition changes hands.
ex.e14: Play as White and find the best move. All the pawns are blocked, on the a and g files. Your king is on e3 and the black king is on d7. Whoever has to move first gives up ground.
ex.e14.hint: The white king must lose a tempo without approaching the black king at once. If it advances right away, Black draws.
ex.e14.solution: 1.Kd3! is the waiting move: the king loses a tempo, and now Black has to move. 1.Ke4? and 1.Kd4? bring the king up too early and only draw. After 1...Kd6, 2.Kd4! takes the direct opposition; after 2...Ke6, 3.Ke4! repeats the opposition with Black to move. With no pawn moves, Black keeps giving up ground, and the white king enters on the chosen wing.
ex.e15: Play as White and find the best move. The f-pawns are blocked and each king protects its own. On the b-file there are three empty squares between the pawns.
ex.e15.hint: Count the empty squares between the b-file pawns. After your move, the number must be even.
ex.e15.solution: 1.b3! leaves two empty squares, b4 and b5, an even number. 1.b4? leaves only one and loses: after 1...b5, the pawns are blocked and it is your king that has to move. After 1.b3 b5, 2.b4 closes the gap and Black is in zugzwang: 2...Kd4 abandons f5, and 3.Kxf5 wins the pawn and the ending.
ex.e16: Play as White and find the best move. The black king is close to the h3 pawn, and yours is far from both pawns. There is one empty square between the a-file pawns.
ex.e16.hint: Before taking the king anywhere, take away Black's last pawn move on the a-file: fix the a5 pawn.
ex.e16.solution: 1.a4! fixes the a5 pawn: Black has no pawn move left on the a-file. 1.Ke7? a4! gives Black the last reserve tempo, and Black wins. After 1...h5, 2.Ke6! Kh4 3.Ke5 (3.Kf5 also works) Kxh3 4.Kf4! Kg2 5.Kg5! Kg3 6.Kxh5. The white king captures the h5 pawn, and the draw is certain, because the a-file pawns are fixed.
part.waiting.title: Waiting with kings
part.waiting.summary: If bringing the king closer stalemates the opponent, wait with the king; spend your pawn move only after he has spent his.
part.fixedTarget.title: Fix first
part.fixedTarget.summary: First blockade the pawn that would give the opponent a spare move: without it, the turn does not change, and your king reaches the defence in time.
part.secondReserve.title: Save a tempo
part.secondReserve.summary: A pawn on the second rank gives two waiting moves if it advances one square at a time; save the second for when the king needs to change the turn.
ex.e14.r1: The black king goes to d6, facing your king. The pawns are blocked: only the kings can wait.
ex.e14.r2: The black king goes to e6, trying to keep pace with the white king. Black has no pawn move.
ex.e15.r1: The black pawn advances to b5 and leaves only one empty square, b4. The white pawn enters it and closes the gap.
ex.e15.r2: Black is in zugzwang: with no pawn move, its king has to move. It goes to d4 and leaves the f5 pawn undefended.
ex.e16.r1: The black pawn advances to h5 and the black king threatens to capture the h3 pawn. The white king hurries to the kingside.
ex.e16.r2: The black king goes to h4, next to the h3 pawn. The white king keeps heading for the h5 pawn.
ex.e16.r3: The black king captures the h3 pawn. Now the white king chases the h5 pawn.
ex.e16.r4: The black king goes to g2 and tries to get back near the h5 pawn.
ex.e16.r5: The black king goes to g3, but it does not protect the h5 pawn.
title: Waiting moves
summary: Changing the turn with a spare pawn move or a king waiting move, to keep the opposition and force the enemy king to give way.
history:
In many pawn endings what decides is not who has the closer king, but who is forced to move first. A pawn that can still advance without consequences is a spare tempo: it lets you pass the move to the opponent. A king move that changes nothing, made only to wait, is a waiting move. Whoever can count these moves turns a seemingly equal position into a win or a draw.

The Soviet master {{Nikolai Grigoriev|nikolai-grigoriev}} composed famous studies on the theme in the early twentieth century, in which two pawns and two kings seem frozen and yet only one precise waiting move keeps the result.
practice: Now the real ending: king on e1, pawn on f3, and the black king on c8. Bring the king in front of the pawn, toward the key squares e5, f5 and g5, and use the opposition to reach one of them. Pick your pace and go.
key.grigoriev: A study by {{Nikolai Grigoriev|nikolai-grigoriev}}, from 1933. Black keeps the advance of the d5 pawn in reserve, a move to change the turn whenever convenient. White needs waiting moves that still work after the reserve is spent.
ex.e20: Play as White and find the best move. Both kings are on the kingside, far from the queenside pawns, and the b6 pawn can still advance. Choose the king route that saves the game.
ex.e20.hint: Do not rush for the pawn: take the king up one file and keep it side by side with the black king, always with one square between them.
ex.e20.solution: 1.Kh2! climbs the h-file. After 1...Kf2, 2.Kh3! keeps the kings side by side; after 2...Kf3, 3.Kh4! and, after 3...Kf4, 4.Kh5! As long as your king follows the black king like this, it cannot get in, and the draw is secured.
ex.e20.r1: The black king climbs the f-file, trying to get ahead.
ex.e20.r2: The black king keeps climbing, always one file beside the white king.
ex.e20.r3: The black king reaches the fourth rank, and the white king still follows it.
ex.e21: Play as White and find the best move. Each side has one pawn still to move and the kings are close. Think about who runs out of pawn moves to pass the turn.
ex.e21.hint: One side has a pawn move that can be spent now or later. Decide which side should spend it first.
ex.e21.solution: 1.b5! locks the structure and forces Black to spend the pawn move; after 1...b6, nobody has a free pawn move left. Then 2.Kd2! prepares the opposition; after 2...Kc4, 3.Kc2! and, after 3...Kb4, 4.Kb2! Your king follows the black king and the draw is secured.
ex.e21.r1: Black spends the pawn move it was saving; now only the kings can move.
ex.e21.r2: The black king climbs to c4, trying to enter through the centre.
ex.e21.r3: The black king goes to b4, aiming at the b5 pawn.
ex.e22: Play as White and find the best move. The black king is on the edge, on h7, and each side has an a-file pawn. Find the move that takes the reserve away from Black.
ex.e22.hint: Whoever can still move the a-file pawn has a reserve move. Stop Black from using theirs when it needs it.
ex.e22.solution: 1.a5! advances the pawn and takes away the pawn move Black would use to pass the turn. After 1...Kh8, 2.Kg6 and the white king reaches the a6 pawn; the win is certain.
coach.allPartsDone: Now you know how to use a waiting move to hand the move back to your opponent. Shall we go to the final test?
ex.e17.hint: If the king moves, the opposition passes to Black. Look for a move that is not a king move and passes the turn.
ex.e17.solution: 1.d6! is the reserve tempo: the pawn passes the turn and the kings stay where they were, with the opposition yours. The black king stays within reach of the pawn, but no move saves it. After 1...Ke8, 2.Ke6! escorts the pawn; after 2...Kd8, 3.d7! Kc7 4.Ke7! and the pawn promotes on d8. A king move, such as 1.Ke5?, gives up the opposition and only draws.
ex.e17.r1: Black has to move the king and goes to e8. The opposition stays with White.
ex.e17.r2: The black king retreats to d8, in front of the pawn, but the white king escorts it.
ex.e17: Play as White and find the best move. The kings face each other on the f-file, with one square between them, and it is your move. Your d5 pawn is next to your king.
ex.e23: Play as White and find the best move. The kings are in front of the central pawns, and your king defends the e4 pawn.
ex.e23.hint: Any king move leaves the e4 pawn undefended. Look for a move that is not a king move: it works as a spare tempo.
ex.e23.solution: 1.b4! is the spare tempo: it passes the turn without moving the king. Now Black is in zugzwang. The black king cannot go to f5, which the e4 pawn controls, and any other square abandons the e5 pawn: after 1...Kf3, 2.Kxe5 and White wins. A king move such as 1.Kc4? or 1.Ke6? leaves the e4 pawn undefended, and 1...Kxe4 draws.
ex.e24: Play as White and find the best move. The black king is in the a8 corner, and the b6 pawn is close to promotion. Beware of stalemate: choose your king's square carefully.
ex.e24.hint: Coming too close takes away every square from the black king. Leave it one free square, and advance the pawn when the black king steps out of the corner.
ex.e24.solution: 1.Kc6! waits and leaves the black king the b8 square. 1.Kc7? is stalemate at once: the black king has no move, and the game is drawn. After 1...Kb8, 2.b7! advances with the black king out of the corner; after 2...Ka7, 3.Kc7! guards b8, and the pawn will promote. If 3.b8=Q+?, 3...Kxb8 captures the queen and draws.
ex.e24.r1: The black king leaves the corner by the only free square.
ex.e24.r2: The black king goes to a7, the only square it has left.
ex.e17.r3: The black king goes to c7 and attacks the d7 pawn; the white king protects it.
